prompt.context: Our client is an Indonesian bank that was privatized three years ago. The bank focuses on retail banking and its clientele is the lower/middle class. The management team is planning regional expansion and their current target market is Singapore. They have asked for advice regarding how to enter the market.
prompt.question: The client wants to know: (1) What kind of customers they should pursue in Singapore? (2) What kind of services they should provide? (3) What is the market size? (4) How should they go after the target customers?

clarifying_info.q: How many banks are currently serving the Singapore market?
clarifying_info.a: There are 3 local banks serving the general population and 6 foreign banks targeting affluent people.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current banking penetration in Singapore?
clarifying_info.a: 80-90% of the Singapore population already has a checking account.

clarifying_info.q: Are Singaporeans likely to switch their deposit or checking accounts?
clarifying_info.a: People generally are not interested in switching their deposit and checking accounts.

clarifying_info.q: Is there interest in asset or wealth management products?
clarifying_info.a: They are not interested in asset/wealth management.

clarifying_info.q: What about car loans or auto financing?
clarifying_info.a: Because of high taxes in Singapore, demand for car purchases is low.

clarifying_info.q: What share of the Singapore population is lower income?
clarifying_info.a: The lower income class of Singapore is about 30% of the population.

framework: Market Segmentation: Identify which customer segment the client can realistically win given existing competitive landscape (3 local banks for general population, 6 foreign banks for affluent) — focus on lower/middle income segment matching existing expertise

Service Differentiation: Determine which product the client can offer that is underserved — systematically eliminate checking/deposits (low switching), wealth management (no demand), auto loans (low demand due to taxes), then identify short-term/signature loans as the gap
Market Sizing: Estimate total addressable revenue from the target segment using population-based approach
Go-to-Market / Execution: Define how to acquire customers and deliver the service efficiently at scale, drawing on Fannie Mae standardization model

questions.prompt: What kind of customers should the Indonesian bank pursue in Singapore?
questions.guidance: The bank should continue focusing on its expertise and serve the lower/middle income segment. The 3 local banks serve the general population and 6 foreign banks target affluent customers, leaving the lower/middle income segment relatively underserved. This also aligns with the bank's existing competency.

questions.prompt: What kind of service should the bank provide?
questions.guidance: Through a structured conversation narrowing down product options: checking/savings accounts are unattractive because 80-90% penetration and people do not switch; wealth management is unattractive because no demand from lower income; auto loans are unattractive because high taxes suppress car purchases. Short-term (signature) loans emerge as the differentiating product for the lower income segment, which typically lacks access to credit from established banks.

questions.prompt: Estimate the market size for the target product.
questions.guidance: Use a population-based approach. Total addressable revenue = Total Singapore population x 30% (lower income share) x average credit line per person x 18% (average APR for signature loans). The average credit line can be estimated as a multiple of average monthly income. Candidate should state assumptions clearly for population and income figures.

math.setup: Market size (annual interest revenue) = Total population x 30% x (average monthly income x credit-line multiplier) x 18% APR
steps: Assume average monthly income for lower income ~SGD 1,500; credit line = e.g. 3x monthly income = SGD 4,500
Total credit extended = 1,200,000 x SGD 4,500 = SGD 5.4 billion (if fully penetrated)
Annual interest revenue = SGD 5.4 billion x 18% = SGD 972 million (upper bound at full penetration)
math.answer: Approximately SGD 1 billion annual interest revenue at full penetration of the lower income segment; candidate should size the realistic capture rate to get an addressable figure

questions.prompt: How should the bank go after the target customers?
questions.guidance: Similar to what Fannie Mae did for the mortgage market, the bank can standardize its short-term loan products. Standardized procedures speed up the approval process, reduce the number of employees needed, and require fewer physical branches. This lowers cost to serve the lower income segment profitably. Key elements: standardized credit scoring/underwriting, streamlined branch or digital application process, lean staffing model.

recommendation: The Indonesian bank should enter Singapore targeting the lower/middle income segment (approx. 30% of population) with a standardized short-term/signature loan product, a segment underserved by existing local and foreign banks
Adopt a Fannie Mae-style standardization model for loan products to drive efficiency, reduce headcount, and minimize branch footprint
risks: Credit risk: the lower income segment has higher default rates; robust underwriting and credit scoring are critical
Regulatory risk: entering a new market requires compliance with MAS regulations and licensing requirements
Reputational risk: any missteps in a foreign market can damage the brand in the home market of Indonesia
next_steps: Conduct market research to validate short-term loan demand and pricing sensitivity in the lower income Singapore segment
Engage with MAS to understand licensing and capital requirements for a foreign retail bank
Design standardized loan product and underwriting process before launch
Pilot with a small branch or digital channel before full rollout
